questions.q: Why does the lesson say a repository containing only raw code is NOT yet a portfolio piece?
options: Because raw code always contains security vulnerabilities
It's still working files -- a portfolio-ready version needs a README, a readable report, presentation slides, and the final dataset/run log
Because code is never allowed to be part of a portfolio
Because portfolios must be submitted as a single PDF file only
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists what needs to be added beyond raw code -- an orienting README, the readable report, both presentation versions, and the final dataset/run log -- to make it a true portfolio piece.

questions.q: What should a strong capstone README state at the very top, in order, per this lesson?
options: The full methodology section, in complete technical detail
The complete limitations section before anything else
What question was investigated, what was found (with the headline number), and how the repository is organized
A list of every contributor's academic credentials
questions.explain: The lesson specifies this exact order for the top of the README: the question, the finding with its headline number, then the repo's organization -- everything else comes after this orienting summary.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say presentation slides in a portfolio package need captions and labeled axes, more so than slides used in a live talk?
options: A portfolio slide deck needs to work as a leave-behind document even without the presenter's narration
Because portfolio slides are never actually viewed by anyone
Because live talks never need any labels or captions at all
Because labeled axes are required by presentation software by default
questions.explain: The lesson explains that without the presenter narrating, captions and labels become more important for the slides to stand on their own as a leave-behind document.

questions.q: Why should the data and run log be stored in a plain, inspectable format (CSV, JSON) rather than requiring your own analysis code to read?
options: Because plain formats are always smaller in file size
So someone trying to verify or extend the work can read the raw numbers directly, without depending on your specific code
Because CSV and JSON are the only formats quantum hardware providers support
Because analysis code should never be shared publicly
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a plain, self-explanatory format lets a visitor inspect the raw numbers directly, serving the goal of making the project legible to someone trying to verify or extend the work.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect directly to Chapter 6?
options: Chapter 6's portfolio-building and interview-preparation lessons assume a packaged asset exactly like the one built in this lesson already exists
This lesson and Chapter 6 are unrelated topics with no connection
Chapter 6 requires starting an entirely new capstone project from scratch
Chapter 6 only applies to students who choose not to complete a capstone
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that a finished capstone only does professional work for you once it's packaged this way, and that Chapter 6 assumes exactly this kind of ready asset exists to point to.
